opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Leila. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. My company would want me on message in public, so I'll give you both versions where they differ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI has made our simulation runs much faster, and that's good for the business. Which is true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get more done. I run more cases in a week than I used to in a month. The bigger question for me is still what happens to oil demand over the next twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep building new tools into how my team works. Keep reading up on carbon storage, since that's where reservoir skills might go next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already live in.

S0.say: AI has made our simulation runs much faster, and that's good for the business.
S0.think: I get more done. The bigger question for me is still what happens to oil demand.
S0.do: Builds new tools into her team's work and keeps reading up on carbon storage as a next step.
S0.feel: Calm. It's the world she already lives in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a sensible pace. It gives companies and people time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer graduate hires is a real problem for our field. We already struggle to bring young engineers into oil and gas. For me personally, ten years is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mentor the juniors we do hire harder, so the few we have are good. Keep my own skills sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit worried for the profession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd call it a sensible pace in public. Is that what you actually think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time, yes. Slow is the best case.

S1.say: It's a sensible pace. It gives companies and people time to adjust.
S1.think: Fewer graduate hires hurts the profession, but ten years is fine for me.
S1.do: Mentors the juniors her team does hire and keeps her own skills sharp.
S1.feel: Fine, a bit worried for the profession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say new roles are opening up and the industry needs to retrain people. That's the line my company would want, and I'd mostly agree with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine office work isn't really my job. Mine is judgement on messy data. I'd be the one directing the agents, probably running a smaller team that does more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put my hand up to lead the AI rollout in reservoir work. Get my name on it. That's the safest seat in the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit excited, which I wouldn't admit at the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you admit that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because some of the people I'd be helping replace sit three desks away.

S2.say: New roles are opening up, and the industry needs to retrain people.
S2.think: My job is judgement on messy data. I'd be directing the agents, with a smaller team that does more.
S2.do: Volunteers to lead the AI rollout in reservoir work so her name is on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say engineering judgement still matters and someone has to sign off. That's what everyone in my position would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it matches skilled professionals, it matches me. I'd like to think I'm in the last group to go, and I probably am. But last isn't never. Our shares and our house would be up, so we'd be fine for money either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make sure I'm the person who signs off on what the AI produces. Move more of our savings somewhere solid. Keep the kids' school funds topped up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared. More like the ground got softer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine for money either way. So what's the unease about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who I am, I suppose. I've been the expert in the room for fifteen years. I'd miss that more than the salary.

S3.say: Engineering judgement still matters, and someone has to sign off.
S3.think: If it matches skilled professionals, it matches me. I'm probably among the last to go, but last isn't never.
S3.do: Makes herself the one who signs off on AI work, and moves savings somewhere solid.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like the ground got softer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before. Engineering judgement matters, and someone has to sign off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots don't change much for me directly. My work is on a screen. If anything, robots in the field make the whole industry cheaper to run. The energy transition still worries me more than any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same as the last one. I'd also look at robotics companies working in oil and gas, both as an investment and as somewhere I might work later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same. Uneasy, but steady.

S4.say: Engineering judgement matters, and someone has to sign off.
S4.think: Robots don't change much for me. The energy transition still worries me more than any of this.
S4.do: Keeps to her plan and looks at oil and gas robotics firms as an investment and a possible future employer.
